subject: History of USA
title: 4. Territorial Expansion and Growth to Fifty States

segments.text: Every new territory raised questions about Indigenous sovereignty, slavery, and diplomacy together — this is simultaneously a map topic and a conflict topic, and the syllabus’s own printed date range (“1820–1949”) is a historical error this resource corrects explicitly.

blocks.text: From Louisiana to the Mexican Cession

segments.text: The Louisiana Purchase (1803) opened vast western lands but intensified conflict with Indigenous nations; the
Adams-Onís Treaty
transferred Florida from Spain (formal transfer 1821). The
Indian Removal Act (1830)
and forced migrations such as the Cherokee
Trail of Tears
reveal the coercive human cost of territorial growth, which should never be presented as a neutral or purely triumphant process.
Texas
declared independence from Mexico in 1836 and was annexed in 1845, contributing to the
Mexican-American War
; the
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)
transferred a huge area to the United States, immediately intensifying the political struggle over whether slavery could expand into western territories (directly feeding into Topic 6).

blocks.text: Oregon, Alaska, Hawaii, and the Real Statehood Dates

segments.text: The Oregon boundary was settled with Britain in 1846, Alaska was purchased from Russia in 1867, and Hawaii was annexed in 1898 — expansion involved diplomacy as well as war. Correcting the syllabus heading precisely:
Alaska became the 49th state on 3 January 1959 and Hawaii the 50th on 21 August 1959
, not by 1949 as the official FPSC date range states.

items.text: The nineteenth-century belief that continental expansion was justified or inevitable — an ideology to analyse critically, not a neutral historical fact, given its consequences for Indigenous peoples and Mexico.

segments.text: Preparation Checklist

items.text: Draw a territorial-acquisition map; for each acquisition record date, method, territory gained and consequence; add a separate section on Indigenous dispossession and one on how expansion worsened the slavery dispute.

segments.text: Common Confusions to Avoid

items.text: Do not present Manifest Destiny as a neutral fact; it was an ideology with serious consequences for Indigenous peoples and Mexico.
Do not say the U.S. had 50 states by 1949; Alaska and Hawaii entered in 1959.
Do not treat territorial expansion as separate from the slavery crisis; new lands repeatedly reopened the issue.

segments.text: Easy Revision Points

items.text: Texas was annexed in 1845; the Mexican-American War (1846–48) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
The United States acquired Alaska from Russia (1867) and annexed Hawaii (1898).
The official FPSC heading’s date range is inaccurate: Alaska became the 49th state and Hawaii the 50th in 1959, not 1949.
Correct the syllabus’s own date-range error explicitly in any answer: the 49th and 50th states joined in 1959, not by 1949.
Treat expansion as simultaneously a diplomatic/territorial story and a conflict story — Indigenous dispossession and the slavery-expansion dispute are integral, not footnotes.
